extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and scholars of social science and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for constructing and evaluating scientific inquiry into social and political phenomena, emphasizing the relation between psychology (individual laws) and ethology (social deductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification a posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: The inference given by theory as to the type of character or social effect which would be formed by any given circumstances must be tested by specific experience of those circumstances whenever obtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory cannot be trusted unless confirmed by observation; observations are not sufficient unless they can be affiliated to theory. The consilience of a priori reasoning and specific experience is the sufficient ground for principles in complex sciences like Ethology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer to obtain the highest generalizations first when induction conditions permit
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositions afterward recognized as the most general truths of a science are often those earliest arrived at, because where causes are accessible the simplest cases (fewest causes) elicit laws of greatest comprehensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertain first those general laws for which real induction can most completely be realized — typically the simplest cases where causes are few — and deduce middle principles from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology must be a deductive science founded on psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethology, the deductive science of the formation of character and social effects, is a system of corollaries from Psychology, the experimental science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct ethological deductions from general psychological laws and then verify them against empirical materials (historical and contemporary observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form middle principles from general laws of psychology for practical art
rubrics_metrics.description: The great problem of Ethology is to deduce the requisite middle principles from the general laws of Psychology so as to determine what combinations of circumstances promote or prevent qualities of human character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these middle principles, arranged by desirable or preventable effects, as the foundation for practical arts (e.g., education), adapting precepts to individual circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social science should explain causes rather than propose universal precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many political writers attempted to frame universal precepts (one form of government to fit all cases), but the phenomena of society, though governed by laws, admit of so many varying circumstances that universal practical maxims are generally impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to establish general laws and understand causal mechanisms; accept that art/policy must adapt measures to particular circumstances rather than apply one-size-fits-all rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes: reduce social phenomena to laws of individual human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: All phenomena of society are phenomena of human nature generated by outward circumstances acting on masses; human beings in society have no properties but those derived from the laws of the nature of individual man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground social explanations in the laws of individual motives and actions; do not treat society as a fundamentally different substance with independent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the Chemical/Experimental mode for social inquiry when causes are multiply compounded
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chemical mode proceeds as if the nature of man as individual were of little concern and demands specific experience in every case; this is inappropriate because social phenomena involve a complication of causes that precludes true experimental control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to reason from single unanalyzed historical instances or unreplicated experiments; recognize the logical impossibility of artificial experiments and of meeting conditions required for conclusive induction in social science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference requires instances differing only in the factor under inquiry — rarely possible in social science
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply the Method of Difference we require two instances which tally in every particular except the one under inquiry; such a concurrence (e.g., two nations identical except in tariff) is manifestly impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on putative method-of-difference 'experiments' drawn from history unless one can demonstrably eliminate all other differing antecedents — which in practice is not attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference (comparing classes) is inconclusive due to multiple contributing causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing one nation with several others each matching in different subsets of circumstances gives only specious semblance of conclusiveness because prosperity may result from many co-operating circumstances not equally shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sceptical of arguments that infer causation from comparisons of heterogeneous classes unless you can account for the many interacting favorable factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement is weak where plurality of causes prevails
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding several instances that agree only in one antecedent is insufficient to infer that antecedent caused the effect when the effect can have multiple causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that elimination of some antecedents only shows the effect can occur without them, not that the remaining antecedent is the necessary or sole cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations fails when aggregate effects derive from many interacting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If attributes of the social body are influenced by innumerable causes, variations in the aggregate cannot bear uniform proportion to variations in any single component cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect neat proportional relations between a single social cause and aggregate social outcomes; causal inferences from concomitant variations will be unreliable in such complex systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues presupposes known causes learned by deduction from human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Residues subtracts effects of known causes to attribute the remainder to other circumstances, but applied to social phenomena it presupposes that some causes are already known — which must come from deduction from principles of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Method of Residues only as a supplement to deductions from psychological principles; it cannot stand alone as a purely empirical method in social science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give preference to simplest cases where fewest causes operate for inductive work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where our means of investigation can reach causes without stopping at empirical laws, the simplest cases (fewest causes) will be most amenable to the inductive process and will elicit the most comprehensive laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting phenomena for inductive study, prioritize situations with minimal causal complexity to maximize the reliability of generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consilience of a priori reasoning and specific experience is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The accordance of a priori reasoning and specific experience—which separately taken are insufficient—forms the only sufficient ground for the principles of a science dealing with complex and concrete phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure theoretical deductions from human nature are tested against well-collated empirical instances; accept principles only where both lines of evidence converge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reasoning from single historical examples or casual coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that draw general conclusions from a single unanalyzed instance or from unexamined historical analogies (Athens, Rome, etc.) are invalid because they fail to analyze antecedents and eliminate confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require careful analysis and comparison of instances, not mere citation of famous historical cases, before generalizing causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of prediction but value of causal understanding for guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when laws are known, the innumerable and changing data in social affairs limit long-range prediction; nevertheless, knowledge sufficient to explain causes, tendencies, and to guide modification or prevention of effects is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social-scientific work by its ability to explain past states, indicate tendencies, and suggest means to alter outcomes given well-understood individual and contextual data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate deductive social science with geometry-like abstract deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some thinkers assimilate deductive social science to geometry, ignoring that causal sciences must accommodate conflicting forces and interacting causes, unlike geometry's co-existent and non-interactive relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forms of deduction suited to causal, dynamic systems (more like mechanics/astronomy) rather than the purely axiomatic, conflict-free model of geometry.
